library.name: Process Hollowing & Cobalt Strike Beacon Loader
library.shortSubtitle: Malware Analysis · svchost.exe Memory Unmapping & PE Injection
library.overview: Imagine an intruder who wants to enter a high-security bank without raising an alarm. Instead of breaking down the front door in a ski mask, they hire an official armored bank truck, freeze it inside the garage before the driver even starts the route, and pocket two golden master keys: the first master key unlocks the rear cargo doors so they can empty all the legal bank gold and load their own covert crew inside, and the second master key unlocks the driver cab so they can reprogram the GPS route and release the brake. When the truck rolls out, every security camera and guard at the gate still sees the bank’s own trusted license plate and uniform. In this scenario (T1055.012, Process Hollowing & Cobalt Strike Beacon Loader) on WKS-04 (10.10.4), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: launching a Legitimate Windows Process, then hollowing Out the Original svchost.exe Code, then allocating Writable-Executable Memory, then hijacking the CPU Thread Context. Steps #1–#5 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Launching a Legitimate Windows Process, then Hollowing Out the Original svchost.exe Code, then Allocating Writable-Executable Memory, then Hijacking the CPU Thread Context, then Outbound HTTPS Command-and-Control Beacon. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

library.name: Log4Shell JNDI Injection to Reverse Shell (DFIR Log Trace)
library.shortSubtitle: Network & Web DFIR · Web Access Logs, Rogue LDAP, Java Spawning Bash & Auditd
library.overview: A hotel reception clerk writes every guest badge note verbatim into a smart ledger that automatically phones any directory number printed on the paper. A visitor hands over a slip listing an outside phone bureau, so the clerk dials out, fetches an unsigned instruction booklet from a street kiosk, and hands the master phone line to the caller. In this scenario (CVE-2021-44228, Log4Shell JNDI Injection to Reverse Shell) at 10.20.1, the attacker plants a malicious lookup string so a helpful logger dials out and loads remote code instead of writing plain text. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: hide a JNDI LDAP lure inside an HTTP header (so the guestbook dials an outside bureau), force Log4j to evaluate that lookup (so the app asks the attacker what to build), follow the LDAP referral to download bytecode (so unsigned instructions enter the JVM), then run the static initializer into a reverse shell (handing the line to the caller). Steps #1–#4 walk that chain end-to-end by covering the poisoned header, outbound LDAP call, remote class load, and shell spawn, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible. Primary detection pivots on Suricata and nginx access-log telemetry across the kill chain.

Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Sending an Unsigned "alg": "none" OAuth JWT, then Minting a Second "alg": "none" JWT, then Importing a Malicious BCS .bdcm, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. On a Windows workstation (MITRE T1003.001), an attacker enables debug privileges, then uses the signed comsvcs.dll MiniDump export through rundll32 to snapshot lsass.exe memory into an on-disk MDMP file without loading a known credential-theft tool. Steps #1 cover privilege adjustment and process discovery in Security logs, Step #2 analyze cross-process OpenProcess and MiniDump calls in Sysmon EventID 10, and Step #3 verify the minidump header and offline credential parsing from file-create telemetry. Primary detection pivots on Sysmon process access to lsass.exe with broad GrantedAccess masks and a CallTrace that includes comsvcs.dll or MiniDumpWriteDump.

Stage 2: Cross-Process OpenProcess & MiniDumpWriteDump via comsvcs.dll (Sysmon EventID 10)

library.name: Microsoft MSTIC & SANS DFIR — Scheduled Task Creation & TaskCache SD Descriptor Deletion (EventID 4698 / Sysmon EID 12)
library.overview: Imagine an intruder who posts a recurring work shift onto the building official wall calendar, then sneaks back with supreme master keys to rip off the permission label from that calendar index card so the public shift viewer becomes blind and refuses to list the job. Despite the clever invisibility trick, forensic investigators walk straight into the back-room task drawer where the full execution card and execution logbook remain completely intact. In this DFIR walkthrough (MITRE T1053.005 on a compromised Windows server), an adversary registers a SYSTEM scheduled task that launches a payload on a timer, then uses the Tarrask technique to peel the TaskCache index label so schtasks and the Task Scheduler GUI no longer list the job while the engine still runs it. Steps #1 cover lawful task creation logs and on-disk XML, Step #2 covers registry SD deletion and Sysmon alerts, and Step #3 recovers the hidden command line from TaskCache Tasks GUID storage and TaskScheduler run history. Primary detection pivots on pairing Security EventID 4698 with Sysmon registry delete events under TaskCache Tree and hunting GUID-only tasks missing Tree SD values.
